title: Every good gift (James 1:9–18)
hook: every good gift comes from the Father of lights

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first lines of James, count it all joy, and your line was ask for wisdom. Whose advice did you ask for, and did you listen? Day six hundred seventy.

Stand outside on a clear night and watch the sky for an hour. The moon moves. Stars rise in the east and sink in the west. Clouds slide across and shadows shift on the ground. Even the sun, by day, changes the length of every shadow from morning to evening. The lights in the sky are beautiful, but none of them stays put. Ancient people watched them closely and knew it. James is about to use that very picture. But first he has something hard to say about where temptation comes from, and something gentle about where good things come from.

James starts with a reversal. Let the poor believer be proud of being lifted up, and the rich one glad to be brought low, because the rich fade like a flower in the field when the sun's heat rises. Then a blessing: "Blessed is the man that endureth temptation." And then a warning, plain as a sign on a door: "Let no man say when he is tempted, I am tempted of God." Don't blame heaven. Temptation, James says, comes from inside, from our own desire, and it grows like a pregnancy: desire conceives, gives birth to sin, and sin, full grown, brings death. That's a hard image, and James means it to be. But he won't leave it there. "Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning." Father of lights. In Genesis God makes the great lights, the sun and the moon and the stars. So James calls God their father, their maker. And then the contrast with that night sky: the lights move, they wane, their shadows turn, but the one who made them doesn't. No variableness. Neither shadow of turning. God isn't moody. The good doesn't flicker on and off. And notice the direction. The bad grows up from below, out of desire. The good comes down from above, as gift. Then a last surprise: God, of his own will, "begat" us, gave us birth, by the word of truth. Two births in one passage. Desire gives birth to death. God gives birth to us.

Here's the practice: list three good gifts. Settle, and breathe. Think back over the last day or two. Find one good thing you didn't earn: a kindness, a meal, a moment of beauty. Name it. Then a second. Then a third. Take your time with each one, picture it clearly, and then trace it back as far as you can. Who gave it? Who made that possible? Where did that come from? If you pray, you can give thanks to the Father of lights for each. If you don't, simply let yourself receive them again, as gifts. The bell holds the time.
Variableness. The steadiness James gives to God, the Father of lights: with whom there is no variableness, neither shadow of turning, unlike the moving sky.
Your line: from the father of lights. Tonight, step outside or look out a window at the sky, and name one gift from today before you go to sleep. Day six hundred seventy.

howItsDone: James 1:17 is a favorite verse for thanksgiving services and harvest festivals, and many Christians recite it as a reminder that every good thing in their lives is a gift.

fork.setup: you've given in to a temptation. what does James say about blaming God for it?
options: fair enough, God set up the test.
don't: temptation comes from your own desire.
fork.reveal: "Let no man say when he is tempted, I am tempted of God." James traces it inward, to desire, and traces every good gift upward.

original.note: Greek: Father of the lights. a title for God as maker of the sun, moon and stars.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice line about presents.
what it means: every good thing comes down from God, who, unlike the shifting lights he made, never changes.
what a scholar hears: 'Father of lights' recalls the great lights of Genesis 1, and 'shadow of turning' may echo the language of the sky's turning lights.

notes: 'Shadow of turning' (τροπῆς ἀποσκίασμα) may draw on astronomical language; the text of 1:17 has variants. Hedged with 'may'. Confirm.
James 1:18 KJV 'Of his own will begat he us with the word of truth' is paraphrased; the word 'begat' is quoted alone.
The two-births contrast (1:15 and 1:18) is a common commentary observation.
